style_1_icd10.name: Fibromyalgia
style_1_icd10.chapter: XIII. Diseases of the musculoskeletal system / Rheumatology (M00-M99)

style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: ACR Guidelines for Rheumatic Diseases & EULAR Consensus (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: Normalization of serum CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Halt radiographic joint erosion and preserve physical mobility

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Fibromyalgia focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Fibromyalgia.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Fibromyalgia.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Fibromyalgia require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Targeted intervention for severe or refractory Fibromyalgia.
drug_classes.dosing: Specialist-guided dosing with pre-treatment laboratory clearance and structured monitoring.
drug_classes.pearls: Perform required baseline screening (e.g. latent infections, CBC, organ function panels) prior to initiation.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Fibromyalgia.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.
Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.
Perform required baseline screening (e.g. latent infections, CBC, organ function panels) prior to initiation.
Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Avoid NSAIDs in eGFR < 30 mL/min; adjust methotrexate and allopurinol based on renal clearance.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for hepatitis B/C before starting DMARDs or biologics; monitor ALT/AST with methotrexate.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Methotrexate and leflunomide are strictly contraindicated; certolizumab and hydroxychloroquine are preferred.
special_populations.elderly: High risk of NSAID-induced gastrointestinal ulcers, fluid retention, and acute kidney injury; co-prescribe PPI.

style_3_monograph.summary: Fibromyalgia is chronic (long-lasting) condition that causes pain all over the body, fatigue , and other symptoms. There is no cure, but treatments can help with the symptoms. What causes fibromyalgia? The exact cause of fibromyalgia is unknown. Studies of the brains of people with fibromyalgia found that they seem to process pain differently than people who don't have it. They may feel pain when others do not, and they may also have a more severe reaction to pain. Fibromyalgia can run in families, so genetics may also play a role. Other factors may also be involved, such as having certain diseases that cause pain. Who is at risk for fibromyalgia? Anyone can get fibromyalgia, but it is more common in: Women; they are twice as likely to have fibromyalgia Middle-aged people; your chance of having it increases as you get older People with certain diseases, such as lupus , rheumatoid arthritis , osteoarthritis or ankylosing spondylitis People who have a family member with fibromyalgia What are the symptoms of fibromyalgia? The main symptoms of fibromyalgia are: Chronic (long-lasting) pain and stiffness all over the body. People often describe it as aching, burning, or throbbing. Fatigue and tiredness. Trouble sleeping . Other symptoms may include: Problems with thinking, memory, and concentration (sometimes called "fibro fog") Muscle and joint stiffness Numbness or tingling in the arms and legs Sensitivity to light, noise, odors, and temperature People who have fibromyalgia are also more likely to have certain diseases, including: Anxiety Depression Headaches , including migraines Irritable bowel syndrome Pain in the face or jaw, including disorders of the jaw know as temporomandibular joint syndrome (TMJ) How is fibromyalgia diagnosed? Fibromyalgia can be hard to diagnose. It sometimes takes visits to several different health care providers to get a diagnosis. One problem is that there isn't a specific test for it. And the main symptoms, pain and fatigue, are common in many other conditions. Providers have to rule out other causes of the symptoms before making a diagnosis of fibromyalgia. This is called making a differential diagnosis . To find out if you have fibromyalgia, your provider: Will take your medical history, including asking detailed questions about your symptoms Will do a physical exam May order x-rays and blood tests to rule out other conditions What are the treatments for fibromyalgia? Not all providers are familiar with fibromyalgia and its treatment. You should see a provider or team of providers who specialize in the treatment of fibromyalgia. There is no cure for fibromyalgia, so treatment focuses on relieving the symptoms. Providers usually use a combination of treatments, including medicines, lifestyle changes, talk therapy, and complementary therapies: Medicines Certain antidepressants and anti-seizure medicines, which may help with pain or sleep problems. Pain relievers . Lifestyle changes Getting enough sleep . Getting regular physical activity. If you have not already been active, start slowly and gradually increase how much activity you get. You may want to see a physical therapist, who can help you create a plan that is right for you. Learning how to manage stress . Learning to pace yourself. If you do too much, it can make your symptoms worse. So you need to learn to balance being active with your need for rest. Talk therapy , such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), can help you learn strategies to deal with pain, stress, and negative thoughts. If you also have depression along with your fibromyalgia, talk therapy can help with that too. Complementary therapies have helped some people with the symptoms of fibromyalgia. But researchers need to do more studies to show which ones are effective. You could consider trying them, but you should check with your provider first. These therapies include: Mindfulness meditation. Biofeedback, which uses electronic devices to measure body functions such as breathing and heart rate. This teaches you to be more aware of your body functions so you can learn to control them. Movement therapies such as yoga and tai chi. Massage therapy. Acupuncture .
style_3_monograph.treatment: The goals of treatment are to help relieve pain and other symptoms, to reduce disability, and to help the person cope with the symptoms. The first type of treatment may involve: Physical therapy An exercise and fitness program Stress-relief methods, including light massage and relaxation techniques If these treatments do not work, your provider may also prescribe an antidepressant or muscle relaxant. Sometimes, combinations of medicines are helpful. The goal of these medicines is to improve your sleep and help you better tolerate pain. Medicine should be used along with exercise and behavior therapy. Duloxetine (Cymbalta), pregabalin (Lyrica), and milnacipran (Savella) are medicines that are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) specifically for treating fibromyalgia. Other medicines are also used to treat the condition, such as: Anti-seizure drugs, such as gabapentin Other antidepressants, such as amitriptyline Muscle relaxants, such as cyclobenzaprine Pain relievers, such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, or tramadol If you have sleep apnea, a device called continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may be prescribed. Cognitive-behavioral therapy is an important part of treatment. This therapy helps you learn how to: Deal with negative thoughts Keep a diary of pain and symptoms Recognize what makes your symptoms worse Seek out enjoyable activities Set limits Complementary and alternative treatments may also be helpful. These may include: Tai chi Yoga Acupuncture Support groups may also help. Things you can do to help take care of yourself include: Eat a well-balanced diet. Avoid caffeine. Practice a good sleep routine to improve quality of sleep. Exercise regularly. Start with low-level exercise. There is no evidence that opioids are effective in the treatment of fibromyalgia, and studies have suggested possible adverse effects. They should be avoided. Referral to a clinic with special expertise in diagnosing and treating fibromyalgia may be helpful.
